conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here for your autologous stem cell transplant as part of your multiple myeloma treatment. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m okay, a bit tired, but ready to get this done. The last few treatments were rough with the breathing and the shingles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you had some complications with Velcade and then the zoster outbreak. But you’ve recovered well. We’ll be giving melphalan chemotherapy starting in a few days, then reinfusing your stem cells. We’ve placed a central line for access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the line was put in this morning. Is that going to stay in long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s temporary—just for this admission. We’ll remove it before you go home. We also started acyclovir to prevent another shingles flare, and you’ll get pentamidine later for pneumonia prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I don’t want another bout of shingles. My arm’s healing from the skin cancer removal too—dermatology said I need a follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted the squamous cell carcinoma was excised before admission. Important to keep that follow-up in three months. For now, we’ll monitor your counts closely. The melphalan will suppress your bone marrow, so you’ll be neutropenic for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s when I’m most at risk for infection, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we start antibiotics like ciprofloxacin as prevention. But if you spike a fever, we’ll switch to stronger IV antibiotics right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My back’s been bothering me—still on the OxyContin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on 20mg twice daily, with extra oxycodone as needed. We’ll adjust if pain worsens. We saw your recent MRI showed some spinal changes, but no clear tumor involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. And my mood’s better since starting the citalopram again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we restarted citalopram yesterday. It was held during transplant prep. We’ll keep it going for your depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave your melphalan yesterday and today. You’re doing well so far. We’ll start Neupogen soon to help your counts recover after the nadir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mucositis is common—sores in the mouth or throat. We’ll give mouth rinses and pain meds. Also nausea, diarrhea, and fatigue. We’re watching your kidneys and hydration closely, especially with your neobladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the big day—your stem cells are being reinfused. You might feel some chills or nausea during the process, but we’ll manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the last time—felt a bit metallic. Is it the same stuff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same cells collected earlier. We tested them—no growth in culture, so they’re clean. You should start feeling the effects in about a week when your counts hit their lowest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is dropping as expected. We’re keeping you on cipro for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked a fever last night—101.4. We’ve switched you to IV cefepime just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. No cough or urinary symptoms. Blood and urine cultures are pending. We’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today is clear. No pneumonia. Continue cefepime for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked another fever this morning and have some brown sputum. Also, you mentioned trouble swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it hurts to swallow. Feels like something’s stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be mucositis or esophagitis. We’re adding vancomycin, flagyl, and fluconazole to cover all bases—bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot of meds. Will they interact with my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring. We also reduced your OxyContin a bit because you were a little drowsy yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed VRE—vancomycin-resistant enterococcus—but at low levels. Given your neobladder, this is likely colonization, not infection. We won’t treat it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. But you’ll need a urine check in one week after discharge to make sure it doesn’t turn into an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows a new shadow in the right lung. We’re getting a CT scan to check for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the CT shows no pneumonia. But it does show esophagitis, which explains your swallowing pain. The lung shadow was just a shadowing effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in the lungs. But we’re keeping the antibiotics for now since you’re still febrile. We also saw worsening left hydronephrosis—likely from your past surgery. Urology says it’s chronic, but we’ll monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling bloated. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You retained over a liter when we cathed you. We’ll keep a schedule and you can self-cath if you feel full. It helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked a fever again last night. We’re switching fluconazole to caspofungin for broader fungal coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’ve been afebrile since yesterday. Your white count is starting to rise. We’re stopping vancomycin and flagyl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m over the worst of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your body is recovering. We’ll stop cefepime and caspofungin tomorrow if you stay fever-free and your counts keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All antibiotics are now stopped. No organisms grew in your blood cultures. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m eating better. Mouth sores are healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re giving you mouth rinses and saliva substitutes to help. Also, your magnesium is low, so we’re adding supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show improving kidney function. The hydronephrosis is stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I keep cathing at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you feel bloated. As long as you’re urinating and your kidney numbers stay normal, you’re fine. But call if you have pain or can’t pass urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last chest X-ray is clear. You’re breathing well. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acyclovir three times a day, magnesium twice a day, pantoprazole for your esophagitis, and your pain meds. Also, a multivitamin and stool softener as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Coumadin for my atrial fibrillation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your oncologist will restart it when your counts are fully recovered. Don’t start it on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re afebrile, walking, and eating well. We’ll send you home with instructions and a follow-up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to drink more fluids, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at least two liters a day. And straight cath if you feel full. Also, get that urine test done in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dermatology follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in three months. Watch for any new skin changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Keep taking your meds, stay hydrated, and call if you develop fever, trouble breathing, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great through a tough treatment. We’ll see you in the clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—don’t forget the aerosolized pentamidine you got yesterday counts as your first dose. Start Bactrim only when your doctor tells you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No Bactrim yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. And monitor your mood. Keep taking the citalopram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. It’s helping more now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Stay in touch with your care team. You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over everything before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your back pain is stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, manageable with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep using the oxycodone as needed, but don’t exceed the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve learned my lesson with drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. And keep using your inhalers for your COPD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Advair and Spiriva—every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in clinic.
